overview.title: Moneris Go portal
overview.headline: I redesigned the portal merchants use to run their payments, from one-store shops to national chains. [[P13 One-line outcome, e.g. 'Merchants find their sales in X fewer steps' || Merchants now reach their sales totals in 3 steps instead of 7.]]
facts: Moneris, one of Canada’s largest payment processors
Senior Product Designer. Lead designer on some features, collaborating with other designers on others, and sole designer on the rest
Product managers, analysts, developers and fellow designers
About one year. [[P1 Confirm the timeline and phases, e.g. '12 months in 4 phases' || Four phases over 12 months.]]

Navigation and information architecture, reports, transaction details, fraud detection, invoicing, Virtual Terminal, recurring payments, Vault, Visa Installments, terminal settings, sign-in and design system
usertesting.com sessions, client interviews, support ticket analysis, journey mapping, prototyping, accessibility review (WCAG 2.1 AA)
Figma, FigJam, usertesting.com. [[P58 Add only tools you really used, e.g. Jira, Confluence, Miro || Jira, Confluence and Miro.]]

blocks.x: Merchants open this portal to answer the questions that matter to a business. How much did I sell? Where is my money? Was this payment legitimate? Can I take a payment over the phone? A single-location café and a national chain use the same product with the same urgency, but with very different needs and very different payments knowledge.

When I started, the portal had grown one feature at a time. [[P2 One sentence on what was wrong, e.g. 'Screens were built by different teams with different patterns' || Screens had been built by different teams at different times, with different patterns.]] The result for merchants was [[P3 A real consequence, e.g. 'they had to relearn each page, and support heard the same questions again and again' || they had to relearn each page, and support heard the same questions again and again]].

blocks.title: Constraints I designed within
blocks.x: No shared design system existed. Merchants range from one-store shops to large chains. Payments data is dense and must be masked and handled carefully. Everything had to meet WCAG 2.1 AA. Whether I led or worked alongside other designers, every decision had to be explained to product, analysts and developers, not just drawn.
I treated this as a product problem with a design-system answer. The plan had three parts.

items: Listen first. Learn what merchants were trying to do through usertesting.com sessions, client interviews and support tickets, before drawing screens.

Fix the highest-friction flows first. I started with reports and transaction details because [[P4 Why these came first, e.g. 'they had the highest usage and the most support tickets' || they had the highest usage and the most support tickets]].
Build the system as I go. Every redesigned screen fed a shared component library, so each next screen was faster, more consistent and accessible by default.

studies.title: Reports, transaction details and fraud detection
studies.card: Helping merchants answer “how much did I sell?” and “what happened to this payment?”
studies.headline: Merchants get from a question to an answer on one screen. [[P13 Outcome headline, e.g. 'Totals in X fewer steps' || Totals now take 3 steps instead of 7.]]
facts: Senior Product Designer · [[P97 Lead, collaborating or sole designer on this study || Lead designer]]
[[P1 Phase timeline for this study || Phases 1 to 3, months 1 to 8]]
Sales Summary report, monthly and daily summaries, transaction details, fraud detection

blocks.x: Merchants and finance teams use reports to reconcile sales, check what was refunded and know what they will be paid. Large chains filter across many merchants and stores. Small merchants usually want yesterday’s total and nothing else. When a payment is questioned, they need the full story right away: who paid, how, what fees applied and what happened next.

The old reports [[P14 What was wrong, e.g. 'hid key filters and returned tables that were hard to scan' || hid key filters and returned tables that were hard to scan]]. Transaction information was [[P59 How the old transaction detail failed, e.g. 'spread across several views' || spread across several views]].

items: Reporting back-end limits: [[P22 A real data constraint, e.g. 'reports can take up to XX seconds to generate' || large reports can take up to 20 seconds to generate]]
Merchants who handle both CAD and USD
Dozens of transaction fields, many needed for disputes and reconciliation
Cardholder numbers must be masked, for example 4242****4242. [[P29 Any other compliance rule you can share || Full card numbers may never be shown or exported.]]
No design system for tables, filters or date pickers

blocks.x: [[P15 XX || 24]] usertesting.com sessions with [[P15 merchant types || small retailers, restaurants and multi-store chains]], [[P16 XX || 12]] client interviews, and [[P17 XX || 180]] support tickets reviewed and tagged over [[P17 XX months || 6 months]].

items.finding: [[P18 Finding 1 || Merchants could not tell which account or dates a report covered]]
items.decision: [[P18 The decision it caused || Account and date range pinned to the top of every summary]]

items.finding: [[P19 Finding 2 || Most small merchants only wanted yesterday’s total]]
items.decision: [[P19 The decision it caused || Sensible defaults so a report runs in two clicks]]

items.finding: [[P20 Finding 3 || Finance teams re-keyed totals from PDFs]]
items.decision: [[P20 The decision it caused || Highlighted grand totals and a download beside the data]]

blocks.x: [[P21 One real, anonymized merchant quote || I just want to know what I made yesterday and what is coming into my bank. I don’t want to build a report.]]
blocks.who: [[P21 Merchant type, e.g. small business owner || Small business owner, restaurant]]

blocks.label: Sales Summary: filters and summary view
blocks.note: Export the filter screen and the summary view side by side.

items.title: Filter first, then preview
items.chosen: The report starts with one filter screen: merchant or chain, card type, date range and Group by, with Preview and Reset.
items.why: Merchants shape the report before they wait for it.
items.cost: [[P23 The trade-off, e.g. 'one extra step for simple needs, so I added defaults' || one extra step for simple needs, so I added defaults]]

items.title: Always show which account and dates
items.chosen: Account number, account name and date range sit at the top of every summary.
items.why: [[P24 Why, e.g. 'chain users switch accounts constantly and misreading the wrong account is costly' || chain users switch accounts constantly and reading the wrong account is costly]]
items.cost: Uses vertical space on small screens.

items.title: One table per currency, with a clear No Data state
items.chosen: CAD and USD are separated. An empty table says so instead of leaving a gap.
items.why: Mixing currencies makes totals hard to trust.
items.cost: Merchants with one currency see one table, so the layout adapts.

items.title: Totals that stand out
items.chosen: The grand total row is visually distinct from line items.
items.why: Totals are what people reconcile against.
items.cost: None worth noting.

items.title: Three time views
items.chosen: Summary for the whole range, monthly summary and daily summary.
items.why: Owners and finance teams think in different time units.
items.cost: More views to maintain, so they share one table component.

items.title: Export where people look
items.chosen: Save as PDF and download actions sit beside the data.
items.why: Reports are shared with accountants and owners.
items.cost: None worth noting.

sections.title: The decision I’m proudest of: page or modal?

blocks.x: I did not pick the first idea. I designed two full options for transaction details, a full page and a modal, and compared them against written criteria: [[P30 Your criteria, e.g. 'data volume, comparing transactions, small screens' || data volume, the need to compare transactions, and small screens]]. I chose [[P31 Page or modal, and why || the full page, because merchants compare transactions and need room for dense fee data]], aligned with [[P32 Who, e.g. 'the PM and two developers' || the product manager and two developers]].

blocks.label: Transaction details: full page vs modal
blocks.note: Show both options next to each other, then the one you shipped.

items.title: A summary strip first
items.chosen: Merchant number, date and time, card type, masked cardholder number, transaction type and amount sit at the top.
items.why: [[P33 Why, e.g. 'answers the most common questions without scrolling' || it answers the most common questions without scrolling]]
items.cost: Fields in the strip had to be chosen ruthlessly.

items.title: Sections that match how people think
items.chosen: General, Fees, Gateway and Associated transactions, with a sticky side navigation that highlights the current section.
items.why: Merchants arrive with a specific question, such as why they were charged a fee. Long pages need orientation.
items.cost: [[P36 What you gave up, e.g. 'a single flat view of every field' || a single flat view of every field]]

items.title: Fee transparency
items.chosen: A fee table shows each charge with description, rate, flat amount and total, under a header naming the fee method.
items.why: Fees are a top source of confusion. [[P34 Support stat, e.g. 'XX% of tickets were about fees' || In the tickets I reviewed, about 30% were about fees.]]
items.cost: Adds length for transactions with many fees.

items.title: A deliberate Refund action
items.chosen: Refund is the primary action in brand yellow. Save as PDF and View receipt are secondary.
items.why: Refund is the most consequential action, so it must be findable but not accidental. [[P35 What happens on click, e.g. 'a confirmation step with amount and reason' || Clicking Refund opens a confirmation step with the amount and a reason.]]
items.cost: One extra click to refund.

items.title: Associated transactions together
items.chosen: Related payments, refunds and adjustments are listed on the same page.
items.why: People want the full chain without searching.
items.cost: Needs an extra query from the back end.

blocks.x: Refund abuse and unusual patterns are real losses for merchants, and finding them usually meant exporting data and checking by hand. [[P40 How merchants did it before, and the status: shipped, in pilot or in design || Merchants exported data and checked it by hand. Status: in pilot.]]

blocks.label: Fraud detection report builder
blocks.note: Export the builder showing the rules and the fixed footer.

items.title: A guided report builder
items.chosen: Pick a report type, set the rules, choose the account and date range.
items.why: Merchants answer a few questions instead of building a query.
items.cost: Less flexible than free-form filters.

items.title: Rules in plain language
items.chosen: Checkbox rules such as number of refunds at or above a value between 2 and 999, or total refunds exceeding total purchases.
items.why: Merchants should not need fraud-analyst vocabulary.
items.cost: [[P43 Who set thresholds, e.g. 'analysts set limits, developers confirmed feasibility' || Analysts set the thresholds and developers confirmed feasibility]]

items.title: A fixed Reset and Apply footer
items.chosen: Actions stay in view while the form scrolls.
items.why: Merchants can adjust and re-run quickly.
items.cost: Takes a little screen height.

items.title: A home in the main navigation
items.chosen: Fraud detection sits next to the other reports.
items.why: [[P42 Why, e.g. 'a feature nobody finds does not exist' || a feature nobody finds does not exist]]
items.cost: None worth noting.

blocks.x: [[P44 One real story about a disagreement or constraint, 3 or 4 sentences: what was the tension, who disagreed, what you did, how it ended || Analysts wanted twenty rule options and developers could support six. I tested a short and a long form with merchants, and the short one was finished far faster. We launched with three rules and a way to request more, which kept the form simple and kept the analysts on board.]]

[[P25 What you did, e.g. 'contrast checks, keyboard order in the filter, table header associations, errors that do not rely on colour' || contrast checks on every state, a logical keyboard order through the filters, table headers tied to cells, and errors that do not rely on colour]]

studies.title: Invoicing and Virtual Terminal
studies.card: Taking payments by invoice or by phone without needing payments expertise.
studies.headline: Merchants can bill and take payments without leaving the portal. [[P60 Outcome headline, e.g. 'Invoices sent in X steps' || Invoices go out in 4 steps instead of 9.]]
facts: Senior Product Designer · [[P97 Lead, collaborating or sole designer on this study || Lead designer]]
Product manager, developers, [[P61 Compliance or risk partners, if any || compliance]]
[[P62 Timeline for this study || Months 4 to 8]]
Invoice creation and tracking, Virtual Terminal payment entry, card data validation, confirmation states

metrics.label: Time to send an invoice
metrics.value: [[P63 XX sec → XX sec || 190 sec → 75 sec]]

metrics.label: Adoption
metrics.value: [[P65 XX invoices sent in first XX weeks || 1,200 invoices sent in the first 8 weeks]]

blocks.x: Not every payment happens at a counter. Merchants bill customers after a service, take card details over the phone, and need to know whether an invoice was paid. These are complex payment flows with real money and sensitive card data, and merchants often do them infrequently, so they forget the steps between uses.

Before the redesign, [[P66 What merchants did or struggled with, e.g. 'invoices were created outside the portal and payment entry used a dense form' || invoices were created outside the portal and payment entry used one dense form]].

items: Card data must be validated before it is submitted, and errors must be specific
Sensitive data stays masked wherever it is shown
Infrequent users who need the flow to explain itself
[[P67 A real technical or compliance limit, e.g. 'PCI rules limited what could be stored or shown' || PCI rules limited what could be stored or shown on screen]]

studies.title: Recurring payments, Vault and Visa Installments
studies.card: Making stored cards, repeat billing and installment plans easy to set up and safe to change.
studies.headline: Merchants set up repeat billing and installments with confidence. [[P80 Outcome headline || Merchants turn on installments and repeat billing in minutes.]]
facts: Senior Product Designer · [[P97 Lead, collaborating or sole designer on this study || Lead designer]]
Product manager, developers, [[P81 Others, e.g. payments specialists || payments specialists]]
[[P82 Timeline for this study || Months 7 to 12]]
Vault (stored cards), recurring payments, Dynamic Currency Conversion, Visa Installments settings, terminal settings

metrics.label: Feature adoption
metrics.value: [[P85 XX merchants enabled installments || 420 merchants enabled installments in the first quarter]]

blocks.x: Stored cards, repeat billing, currency conversion and installment plans are powerful, and easy to get wrong. A setting that applies to every device in a store can change what hundreds of customers see at checkout. Merchants needed to understand what each option does before they turn it on.
[[P86 What the problem was before, e.g. 'settings were buried, jargon-heavy and gave no sense of impact' || settings were buried, jargon-heavy and gave no sense of impact]]

items: Settings can apply across every device that supports a feature in a store
Merchants using Moneris Checkout configure installments from a control panel
Stored card data must stay protected
[[P87 Another real constraint || card brand rules decide which plan lengths can be offered]]

blocks.x: [[P88 Sessions, interviews or tickets that shaped this study, with numbers || 7 usertesting.com sessions and 3 client interviews]]

items.finding: [[P89 Finding 1 || Merchants did not know a setting applied to every device]]
items.decision: [[P89 The decision it caused || A confirmation that names the scope of the change]]

items.finding: [[P90 Finding 2 || Merchants wanted to know what customers would see]]
items.decision: [[P90 The decision it caused || Plain-language descriptions beside each plan length]]

blocks.x: [[P91 One real, anonymized quote || I need to know what my customers will see before I switch it on.]]

blocks.label: Visa Installments settings
blocks.figma: Figma · Visa installments frames (enabled and disabled states)
blocks.note: Show the enable toggle, the monthly plan checkboxes and the save confirmation.

items.title: Say what a setting does in the setting
items.chosen: The installments panel explains in plain language that merchants choose which monthly plan lengths to display, and activates each choice with a checkbox.
items.why: Merchants decide with the consequence in front of them.
items.cost: More copy on screen.

items.title: Protect against losing changes
items.chosen: Leaving with unsaved edits triggers a confirmation that names the scope, all devices that support installments across the store.
items.why: A change here touches every device, so a silent loss or a silent save would both be costly.
items.cost: One extra step when leaving.

items.title: Clear enabled and disabled states
items.chosen: The feature has a distinct, readable disabled state.
items.why: Merchants must always know whether customers can see installments.
items.cost: Two states per setting to maintain.

items.title: [[P92 Decision about Vault or recurring payments || Show saved cards without exposing them]]
items.chosen: [[P92 What you chose || Cards in Vault show only the brand and last four digits.]]
items.why: [[P92 Why || Staff can find a customer’s card without ever seeing the full number.]]
items.cost: [[P92 What it cost || Edge cases need a support step because full numbers cannot be copied.]]

blocks.x: [[P93 e.g. 'toggle and checkbox states not relying on colour, focus order through settings, announced confirmations' || toggle and checkbox states that do not rely on colour, a sensible focus order through settings, and confirmations announced to screen readers]]
[[P94 Your best result with the number and how it was measured || Setup completion rose from 63% to 92% in usability tests.]]

studies.title: Secure access and the design system
studies.card: One accessible foundation for every screen, and a sign-in that is secure without being hostile.
studies.headline: One consistent, accessible foundation for every screen. [[P46 Outcome headline || One consistent, accessible foundation for 120 screens.]]
facts: Senior Product Designer · [[P97 Lead, collaborating or sole designer on this study || Lead designer]]
Product manager, developers, [[P48 Security partners, if any || the security team]]
Built alongside every other study, [[P1 over XX months || over the full 12 months]]
Sign-in, enrollment, verification, error messaging, component library, documentation

metrics.label: Build benefit
metrics.value: [[P53 XX% faster or XX fewer bugs || 40% faster builds]]

blocks.x: Sign-in had to be secure without frustrating merchants who are not technical. Enrollment had two audiences: people new to Moneris and people who already had an account.

blocks.label: Sign-in and enrollment
blocks.figma: Figma MD2 · nodes 5:252698 (SSO login) and 5:252869 (mobile journey diverter)
blocks.note: Show the login, the verification step and the new vs existing customer diverter.

items.title: A focused login
items.chosen: One clear primary action, with Forgot your password and Create an account visible without hunting.
items.why: People arrive stressed when they are locked out.
items.cost: Less room for announcements.

items.title: A verification code with Remember my device
items.chosen: Merchants confirm with a code, and can choose to remember the device.
items.why: [[P47 Why you balanced it this way || it balances security with convenience for merchants who sign in daily]]
items.cost: [[P48 Who agreed to the trade-off, e.g. 'security team and PM' || the security team and the product manager]]

items.title: A new vs existing customer diverter on mobile
items.chosen: The mobile journey splits at the start.
items.why: People should not fill in a form meant for someone else.
items.cost: One extra choice up front.

items.title: Errors that say how to fix the problem
items.chosen: [[P49 Your error message approach, e.g. 'a specific message plus the next step' || a specific message plus the next step to fix it]]
items.why: Vague errors create support calls.
items.cost: More copy to write and maintain.

blocks.x: No shared system existed, so each page reinvented buttons, tables and filters. I built the system as I redesigned screens, so every component was proven in a real flow before it was documented.
